name: EEPROM

claims.claim_text: The microcontroller that changed development practice was the first one that was neither ultraviolet-erasable nor one-time programmable, using electrically erasable memory so the part could be reprogrammed in place.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was the first microcontroller that wasn't either UV erasable or one time programmable
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Solar Cells, SparkFun, TSMC - The Detroit Debunking

claims.claim_text: What that replaced was genuinely laborious: either remove the chip and put it in an ultraviolet eraser between attempts, or buy a large and expensive in-circuit emulator that stood in for the whole device.
claims.quote_verbatim: you either had to take the chip out, put it in a UV eraser
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Solar Cells, SparkFun, TSMC - The Detroit Debunking

claims.claim_text: The progression of microcontroller program storage runs mask ROM, then one-time programmable, then electrically erasable memory, then flash. Each step traded unit cost for the ability to change your mind after manufacture.
claims.quote_verbatim: it sort of goes mask, OTP, EEPROM, and then flash
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Questioning Everyday Prototyping - Verrucose Vehicle Vitilitigation

claims.claim_text: Mask ROM was programmed by the semiconductor manufacturer as part of chip fabrication, using a mask specific to your code and requiring a minimum order. That is what made it the cheap option at volume and the inflexible one everywhere else.
claims.quote_verbatim: The factory could actually, the manufacturer could factory program the ROM information for you
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Questioning Everyday Prototyping - Verrucose Vehicle Vitilitigation

claims.claim_text: The development loop before in-circuit programming was slow and frightening: debug through a bulky emulator plugged in place of the part, write in assembly because compilers were often unavailable, then send a hex file to the manufacturer and wait.
claims.quote_verbatim: then you'd cross your fingers and you'd create a hex file
claims.episode_title: An Interview with John Day

claims.claim_text: The exposure in that loop was total. A ROM sample arriving six weeks later that did not work left you with no way to debug it and the prospect of paying another mask charge to try again.
claims.quote_verbatim: What do you do if it doesn't work?
claims.episode_title: An Interview with John Day

claims.claim_text: The intermediate technology was the windowed ultraviolet-erasable part, more expensive because of the window itself. The cycle was to erase for around thirty minutes, program, test, and repeat with a code change, working through several parts at once.
claims.quote_verbatim: you'd put those in a UV eraser for maybe 30 minutes
claims.episode_title: An Interview with John Day

claims.claim_text: The commercially decisive move was making electrically erasable parts cheap enough to ship in production rather than only to develop on. That removed both the mask charge risk of a code bug and the ROM lead time from the schedule.
claims.quote_verbatim: rather than have to go to ROM, you could just go to production on EEPROMs
claims.episode_title: An Interview with John Day

claims.claim_text: The corporate version of that story: a company losing money selling commodity memory applied its own memory process to a microcontroller architecture, producing parts the customer could program instead of parts the factory programmed.
claims.quote_verbatim: we applied our EEPROM technology to the microcontroller architecture
claims.speaker: Steve Sanghi
claims.episode_title: Steve Sanghi - Microchip CEO for 31 Years!

claims.claim_text: The cycle time it replaced was sixteen weeks of waiting for factory-programmed parts, during which the code would change and the process would start over. Compressing that loop is what made the architecture take hold.
claims.quote_verbatim: waiting for 16 weeks
claims.speaker: Steve Sanghi
claims.episode_title: Steve Sanghi - Microchip CEO for 31 Years!

claims.claim_text: These are separate fab technologies rather than successive replacements. Decades later the original ROM-based part, the electrically erasable part and a wide range of flash parts all still run through the same fab, each on the process it was designed for.
claims.quote_verbatim: Those were all distinct technologies
claims.speaker: Steve Sanghi
claims.episode_title: Steve Sanghi - Microchip CEO for 31 Years!

claims.claim_text: The classic field failure with windowed parts is light ingress. Ship a product with the erase window uncovered and ambient light finds its way in through vent holes, slowly erasing the memory over years so the product begins misbehaving long after it left the factory.
claims.quote_verbatim: it would slowly over the years erase your EEPROM
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: 555 Contest, Computer Museum, Octopart - The Green Pen Hornswoggle

claims.claim_text: The variants of that failure are all about what was used to cover the window: tape that eventually falls off, paint that ultraviolet penetrates anyway, or a white paper label that passes enough light to do the job slowly.
claims.quote_verbatim: they used a, uh, white label, you know, a white paper label, which actually lets light through
claims.episode_title: Questioning Everyday Prototyping - Verrucose Vehicle Vitilitigation

claims.claim_text: What makes these failures expensive is that a single flipped bit rarely fails cleanly. Instead of an obvious memory fault it produces behaviour that leads the investigation toward some entirely different part of the circuit, and a week disappears into finding one dead bit.
claims.quote_verbatim: the one bit that would fail would be the one that would lead you down the garden path
claims.episode_title: Radiation Chips & Old Package Types - Technocratic Toilet Troubleshooting

claims.claim_text: Long dormancy is its own failure mode. Equipment powered up only once a year can come back with its stored configuration degraded, presenting as a machine that no longer knows what it is and raising unrelated fault indications.
claims.quote_verbatim: the EEPROM on it had, since it was only powered up, like, once a year, had ended up going bad
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Shaun Meehan - Doctiloquent Dove Deployer

claims.claim_text: A part-selection trap worth checking explicitly: designers assume a microcontroller includes a few hundred bytes to a few kilobytes of internal non-volatile storage for constants and settings, and discover late that the specific part chosen does not have any.
claims.quote_verbatim: We just realized that the chip we chose didn't have internal E2 Prom
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Setting Fire To The Tracks

claims.claim_text: Within a single vendor family the low-power variant may include that internal storage while the otherwise identical standard part does not. The premium for the version that has it can be around forty cents, which is substantial at the scale these parts sell.
claims.quote_verbatim: the price difference is, like, 40 cents
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Setting Fire To The Tracks

claims.claim_text: The cheaper answer is usually an external serial memory chip, available for a few cents, rather than upgrading to a more expensive microcontroller variant. Adding a part beats changing the processor when the only thing missing is storage.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's cheaper to just get an external E-squared problem chip than it is to upgrade the micro
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Setting Fire To The Tracks

claims.claim_text: Write endurance decides the technology. Even good electrically erasable memory is rated in the region of a million write cycles, so an application writing hundreds or thousands of times a second needs ferroelectric memory with effectively unlimited endurance and pays for it.
claims.quote_verbatim: even the best, still has, you know, a million write cycles or something like that
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Setting Fire To The Tracks

claims.claim_text: The high voltage needed to erase these cells never went away; it moved inside the package. On-chip boost circuits generate it, so the part runs from an ordinary low-voltage rail and the designer never sees the requirement.
claims.quote_verbatim: You still need, you still need high, high voltages to a race. They just put boost circuits on board
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Questioning Everyday Prototyping - Verrucose Vehicle Vitilitigation

claims.claim_text: A standard use is board identification: an add-on board carries a small memory holding a description of how its pins are used, and the host reads it at boot and configures its pin multiplexing accordingly.
claims.quote_verbatim: the EEPROM that holds information about how the pins are used
claims.speaker: Matt Richardson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Matt Richardson - Raspberry Risorgimento Regent

claims.claim_text: The reason for that mechanism is beginner experience rather than technical necessity. Selecting the right library manually works, but the design goal was that someone attaching a sensor board should be able to plug it in and have it configured at boot without knowing anything.
claims.quote_verbatim: They want to be able to pop it on and have it configured on boot up
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Matt Richardson - Raspberry Risorgimento Regent

claims.claim_text: The production version of the same idea pairs a unique serial number with about ten bytes of writable memory holding a product code, written at the factory on a programming jig, so a system can identify both which type of board is plugged in and which individual unit it is.
claims.quote_verbatim: we would put in the ID code, the product number for that board
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Fake it till you make it

claims.claim_text: Serial numbering can be folded into the existing test step: the automated test writes the serial number to on-board memory and increments it for each board, whether that memory is inside the microcontroller or a separate chip.
claims.quote_verbatim: the test software just increments the serial number each time you do a new board
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Return of the Trade Show Jedi

claims.claim_text: Memory parts with a factory-programmed unique network address solve the unique-identifier problem cleanly, provided you use a different part in each unit. Pulling them from one bag and reusing a single device gives every unit the same address, which defeats the entire purpose.
claims.quote_verbatim: they all got that same Mac address
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Lesnet - Bus Buccaneer Builder

claims.claim_text: Cloning a USB instrument works by copying the memory contents so the counterfeit identifies itself as the genuine product to the host software. The identity lives in a few bytes rather than in the silicon.
claims.quote_verbatim: putting the same EEPROM contents as we put in ours
claims.speaker: Joe Garrison
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe and Mark Garrison - Subtly Spelling SayLeeAy

claims.claim_text: One vendor responded to clones by writing gibberish into the suspect device's memory, bricking it by corrupting the one part that cannot be replaced from the outside. It is an aggressive countermeasure with obvious consequences for anyone misidentified.
claims.quote_verbatim: break the device basically by like writing like gibberish to the EEPROM
claims.speaker: Joe Garrison
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe and Mark Garrison - Subtly Spelling SayLeeAy

claims.claim_text: A widely repeated theory that another vendor detected clones by timing memory reads was simply wrong. The repeated read attempts were a routine check for a failed memory part, which is a useful reminder that inferred intent behind observed behaviour is often invented.
claims.quote_verbatim: we do that test because it, the EEPROM has failed
claims.speaker: Mark Garrison
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe and Mark Garrison - Subtly Spelling SayLeeAy

claims.claim_text: Tamper resistance in payment and gaming hardware is built around erasing the stored secret: conductive meshes are arranged so that drilling into the enclosure shorts a trace and wipes the memory, with battery backup keeping the mechanism live when the device is off.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't stick your screwdriver drill in and then they'll short and erase the EEPROM
claims.speaker: Dmitry Nedospasov
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching with Michael Ossmann and Dmitry Nedospazov

claims.claim_text: The opposite of that design appeared in early mobile phones, where the identity number sat in a socketed memory chip and the connector to the main board used the same eight-pin arrangement as the chip itself. Reprogramming the identity required only unplugging one part, which made riveting the assembly into the chassis pointless.
claims.quote_verbatim: the plug that went onto the main board was actually an eight-pin dill in the same pinout
claims.episode_title: Live from Serbia with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: A memory chip can replace combinatorial logic outright by acting as a lookup table, taking the inputs as an address and returning the output word. It is a legitimate substitution that also sidesteps the logic minimisation techniques usually taught alongside it.
claims.quote_verbatim: how you can recreate that in an EEPROM as a lookup table
claims.speaker: Ben Eater
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ben Eater

claims.claim_text: Before flash, a common development workaround was an emulator that appears to the target system as its memory chip while appearing to the development machine as ordinary writable memory, so code could be iterated without repeatedly burning and erasing physical parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: The computer with assembler, which serves for that development process, sees it as RAM
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Voja Antonic - Gerontogenous Galaksija Genesis

claims.claim_text: In some programmable logic the memory cells are the configuration rather than a store of it: the cells themselves join the logic together, so the device is configured the instant it powers up with no separate bitstream to load.
claims.quote_verbatim: the E-squared prom fuses actually join the logic together
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: This Is Just A Tribute

claims.claim_text: Small serial memories are sold as finished data products rather than blank storage. A six-pin font chip carries multiple character sets and sizes ready to be read out by a microcontroller, which removes the font from the firmware image entirely.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's a little six-pin, yeah, font chip
claims.episode_title: Beware of the Overachievers

claims.claim_text: An unusual programming channel worth knowing about: hold the board against a computer monitor, have the screen blink black and white squares at a pair of light sensors on the board, and the microcontroller rewrites its own stored pattern from what it reads. No programmer or cable is involved.
claims.quote_verbatim: then read it into the, the microcontroller and it rewrites the EEPROM
claims.speaker: Adam Wolf
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Adam Wolf - Brick & Board Biuners

claims.claim_text: A characteristic debugging nightmare is one unset bit in one memory device that an entire chain of behaviour depended on. The countermeasure an engineer without colleagues to check the work relies on is obsessive written notes acting as a second brain.
claims.quote_verbatim: this one bit and this one EEPROM that you forgot to set
claims.speaker: Nash Reilly
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Nash Reilly

claims.claim_text: Before either electrically erasable memory or flash existed, retaining settings meant battery-backed static memory, with a protection switch diverting a rechargeable cell to keep the memory alive. Machines from that era found in storage have invariably lost everything, because the cell died years ago.
claims.quote_verbatim: There was no E squared prom. There was no flash memory
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Tandy Train

claims.claim_text: A neat per-unit configuration flow at production: scan the shipping label, look up in a database which frequency that customer chose, flash it into the device's memory on a pogo-pin bed, then transmit a test signal at that frequency to verify the unit before it is boxed.
claims.quote_verbatim: this is the frequency that we need to flash into EEPROM
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Dunham

claims.claim_text: The part that opened the field to hobbyists executed directly from electrically erasable memory rather than flash, and with one or two kilobytes as the largest available, assembly language was needed simply to get useful speed and fit.
claims.quote_verbatim: 1K or 2K of memory was, like, that was, like, the biggest pick around
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ben Heck(endorn)

claims.claim_text: Reprogrammability alone was not what made the part accessible; cheap programmers for it were. The combination of a chip you could erase electrically and a programmer an individual could afford is what moved microcontrollers out of professional laboratories.
claims.quote_verbatim: you could buy these cheap programmers for them
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Pull The Trigger
